# Git for Marine Technology

> A short, practical git course for marine technology students. Ten chapters of
> plain markdown in `docs/`, each with a runnable Jupyter notebook twin in
> `notebooks/` that executes the same git commands with `!` shell cells. The
> worked example is `hydrostatics.py`, about thirty lines of naval architecture
> for a box-shaped barge.

Key points:

- **The notebooks are the course, and the only copy of it.** There is no
  written-up markdown version of a chapter: one chapter is one
  `notebooks/NN-name.ipynb`. `docs/` holds only `index.md` (the contents) and
  `09-cheat-sheet.md`. Do not reintroduce generated chapter pages.
- Every notebook works in a throwaway directory under `~/git-course/<chapter>/`,
  wiped and recreated by its first cell, so chapters are independent and can be
  re-run from the top at will.
- Remotes, forks and submodule servers are *local bare repositories*, not
  GitHub: students can see that a server is only a repository without a working
  tree. The commands are identical with a real URL.
- **Keep the notebooks simple.** Code cells use only `!git ...`, `%%writefile`
  (to create or change a file), `%cd`, and plain Python for everything else:
  `os.listdir()` instead of `ls`, `print(Path(...).read_text())` instead of
  `cat`, `os.mkdir()`, and `!"{sys.executable}" script.py` to run a script. No
  `printf`, `sed`, `-q` flags, `&&` chains or `git -C`: students should see
  only commands they would type themselves.
- **The notebooks run on Windows, macOS and Linux.** On Windows, `!` runs
  through cmd.exe, so the only shell commands allowed are `git` ones. The
  first cell of each notebook wipes its folder with `shutil.rmtree` and a
  handler that clears git's read-only flag, which Windows needs. This needs
  Python 3.12 or newer (`onexc`).
- Commits that must fail to teach something are marked with a comment
  containing "on purpose".
- The one notebook device: `git -c sequence.editor=true rebase -i
  --autosquash`, because a notebook cannot open an editor. Elsewhere, avoid
  commands that open one (use `-m` and `--no-edit`).
- Submodules from a local path need `git -c protocol.file.allow=always`
  (CVE-2022-39253); real `https://` and `git@` URLs do not.
- Diagrams are mermaid `gitGraph` and `flowchart` blocks, which render on the
  site, on GitHub, and in JupyterLab 4.1 and later.
- The sample code (`hydrostatics.py`) exists only inside the notebooks, written
  with `%%writefile`; there is no separate copy in the repository.

## Pages

- [Index](./): what the course is, the four places a change can be, contents, how to run the notebooks
- [9. Cheat sheet](09-cheat-sheet/): every command in tables, recovery recipes, three habits

## Chapters (notebooks, in `notebooks/`)

- `00-setup.ipynb`: installing git, identity, useful config, how the notebooks work
- `01-commits.ipynb`: `init`, the staging area, `commit`, diffs, `log`, `amend`, `restore`, `.gitignore`
- `02-branches.ipynb`: a branch as 41 bytes, `switch`, what switching does, the graph view
- `03-merging.ipynb`: fast-forward, merge commit and merge base, conflicts and markers, `--abort`
- `04-rebase.ipynb`: replay as copying, interactive rebase, per-commit conflicts, the golden rule, rebase vs merge
- `05-remotes.ipynb`: bare repositories, `remote add`, `push -u`, remote-tracking branches, `fetch` vs `pull`, rejected pushes
- `06-forks.ipynb`: the upstream/origin triangle, what a pull request is, syncing a fork, fork vs clone vs branch
- `07-cherry-pick.ipynb`: backporting one commit, `-x`, ranges, `git cherry`, when not to use it
- `08-submodules.ipynb`: the pin (mode 160000), `.gitmodules`, empty fresh clones, updating the pin, detached HEAD, alternatives
